newsitem.title: KENYA: Tanzania coffee growers demand payment in dollars.
newsitem.headline: Tanzania coffee growers demand payment in dollars.

text.p: Tanzanian coffee growers have demanded that they be paid for their produce in U.S. dollars, in line with the marketing tradition at the twice-a-month auctions, Tanzanian coffee officials and traders said on Wednesday.

"There has been a small wrangle over the payment system. Coffee unions (of smallholders) and the Tanzania Coffee Growers Association (of estates) wanted to be paid in dollars," said a trader in the northern Tanzanian coffee town of Moshi.
"The (Tanzania Coffee Board) delayed in giving a new auction date because of the pressure from unions and the association," added the trader, speaking to Reuters in Nairobi by telephone.
Tanzania Coffee Board Managing Director Edward Sannda told Reuters the problem of system of payments had been resolved.
Traders buy coffee at the Tanzanian auction and pay the coffee board in dollars. Sannda said since invoicing was also in dollars, he saw no trouble in paying growers also in dollars.

"The only problem there is one of currency exchange rates. We are working on that -- to avoid losses on fluctuations. But people can be paid in the currency they want, Tanzanian shillings or U.S. dollars," he added.
Sannda expected the new payments system to be implemented as early as September but he had no exact date yet.

He said there would be two auctions in September but he did not have a schedule of dates. He said it was true that traders were not given the next auction date after the last auction on Thursday "but the matter appeared to be settled".
Sannda said reports from the auctions and coffee fields indicated that quality of coffees on offer showed improvement.
"We have a smaller crop but better crop," Sannda said.
He said buyers now understood that if they did not obtain good quality coffee, they would lose money at the auctions.
"Buyers cannot afford to be careless (with purchases) at a time when (global) prices are falling. Such a mistake would make them go under, it could be very costly," Sannda added.
An official at a leading coffee house said that apart from the wrangle involving payments, he believed perhaps a new date for the next auction had not been given because of quantities.
"One of the key factors is weather. It is quite cold right now. Although coffee is largely ready for harvest, farmers have simply not been able to harvest," the official said.
"Consequently, milling has been delayed. So, perhaps there isn't enough coffee to be offered at auction," he added.
On Monday, Sannda forecast production in (October/September) 1995/96 at 50,000 tonnes, declining to 42,000 tonnes in 1996/97. He also saw a fall in coffee earnings in 1995/96 and 1996/97.
He also expected lower prices of between $1.50 and $2 per kg this year. Comparative prices in the 1994/95 season were between $2.50 and $3.50 per kg.
